q1: SELECT A.PROJECT_ID, ROUND(AVG(B.EXPERIENCE_YEARS), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM PROJECT AS A INNER JOIN EMPLOYEE AS B ON A.EMPLOYEE_ID = B.EMPLOYEE_ID GROUP BY A.PROJECT_ID
q2: SELECT PROJECT_ID, ROUND(SUM(EXPERIENCE_YEARS)/COUNT(*) ,2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM PROJECT A LEFT JOIN EMPLOYEE B USING (EMPLOYEE_ID) GROUP BY PROJECT_ID
q1_prompt_sql: SELECT A.PROJECT_ID, ROUND(AVG(B.EXPERIENCE_YEARS), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM PROJECT AS A INNER JOIN EMPLOYEE AS B ON A.EMPLOYEE_ID = B.EMPLOYEE_ID GROUP BY A.PROJECT_ID
q2_prompt_sql: SELECT PROJECT_ID, ROUND(SUM(EXPERIENCE_YEARS)/COUNT(*) ,2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM PROJECT A LEFT JOIN EMPLOYEE B USING (EMPLOYEE_ID) GROUP BY PROJECT_ID
counterexample: INSERT INTO EMPLOYEE (EMPLOYEE_ID, NAME, EXPERIENCE_YEARS) VALUES (1, 'Employee1', 5), (2, 'Employee2', 10), (3, 'Employee3', 15); INSERT INTO PROJECT (PROJECT_ID, EMPLOYEE_ID) VALUES (1, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3);
explanation: Q1 calculates the average experience years for each project by dividing the total experience years of all employees in the project by the number of employees in that project. Q2, on the other hand, calculates the average experience years for each project by dividing the total experience years of all employees in the project by the total number of projects, not the number of employees in the project.
counterexample_dsp: The difference is triggered when there are multiple projects and the total number of projects is not equal to the sum of the number of employees in each project.
